prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

You are reviewing layouts of one table, all rendered in a real browser with identical content, font, padding and colours; only column widths differ. You do not know who or what produced them. The first image is the content overview (every cell on one line).
Table: [검증] 한국어 · 다단 헤더 (language ko).
Grid: 5 columns × 5 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Merged cells: "지역" spans 1 col × 2 row; "인구 (만 명)" spans 2 col × 1 row; "평균 기온 (°C)" spans 2 col × 1 row.
Per-column content facts (content px at 15px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "지역" · longest unbreakable word 13px · one-line width 91px
  col 2: header "인구 (만 명) › 2013년" · longest unbreakable word 36px · one-line width 49px
  col 3: header "인구 (만 명) › 2023년" · longest unbreakable word 38px · one-line width 51px
  col 4: header "평균 기온 (°C) › 1월" · longest unbreakable word 29px · one-line width 29px
  col 5: header "평균 기온 (°C) › 8월" · longest unbreakable word 31px · one-line width 31px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 357px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 356px.
Fixed: content, font, 15px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

Rate EACH layout independently: "excellent" | "good" | "acceptable" | "poor" | "bad", with a short reason that points at what you see. Then name the best layout(s) (ties allowed), say how confident you are (low/medium/high), and note anything you are unsure about.
Reply ONLY JSON: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"","why":""},"B":{"grade":"","why":""},"C":{"grade":"","why":""},"D":{"grade":"","why":""},"E":{"grade":"","why":""},"F":{"grade":"","why":""}},"best":["letter"],"confidence":"","unsure":""}

log.raw: {"ratings":{"A":{"grade":"acceptable","why":"Most values scan cleanly, but the 2023 year label, temperature group heading and longest region name wrap, weakening the header hierarchy and row label."},"B":{"grade":"poor","why":"The narrow region column breaks every row label, including the longest across three lines, while the 2023 label also wraps; the extra space in the temperature columns does little to help scanning."},"C":{"grade":"poor","why":"Both year labels and the temperature group heading wrap, creating a tall header, and the longest region name also breaks."},"D":{"grade":"poor","why":"Region names and years stay intact, but the narrow final column splits 25.9 across lines, making a numeric value difficult to read and compare."},"E":{"grade":"good","why":"The group headings and all numbers remain intact, though the 2023 label and the longest region name wrap."},"F":{"grade":"excellent","why":"Both header levels and all numbers stay intact, paired columns have balanced widths, and only the longest region name wraps."}},"best":["F"],"confidence":"high","unsure":"The exact break in the longest region name is slightly hard to discern at this image size."}
